summary: Children compute the area of a rectangle by multiplying its side lengths (7 cm × 9 cm = 63 cm²), keeping the array meaning in view (squares in a row × number of rows) and answering in square units. They also work the relationship backwards: given a target area such as 36 square units, they construct rectangles whose side lengths multiply to that area (2×18, 3×12, 4×9, 6×6) and label the sides. Multiplying for area is explicitly contrasted with adding for perimeter so the two measures are not conflated.
misconceptions: Adds the side lengths (perimeter) instead of multiplying for area.
Gives the answer in linear units (cm) rather than square units (cm²).
Cannot reverse the relationship — struggles to draw a rectangle of a given area or to find its factor-pair sides.
Multiplies unrelated numbers or applies l×w to a non-rectangle.

activities.title: Build and compute: side × side = area
steps: Choose two side lengths for a rectangle (e.g. 7 and 9) and draw it on squared paper or with a grid overlay.
Count the squares as rows of squares (squares-in-a-row × number of rows) and confirm this equals multiplying the side lengths: 7 × 9 = 63.
Write the answer with square units: 63 cm².
Change one side (e.g. 7 → 8) and recompute, noticing the rectangle re-tiles and the area becomes 8 × 9 = 72 cm².
Solve a real context: a garden 8 m by 5 m — find its area (8 × 5 = 40 m²).
activities.insight: Multiplying the two side lengths gives the same total as counting all the unit squares, because the rectangle is a number of equal rows; the result is measured in square units.

activities.title: Reverse the relationship: many rectangles, one area
steps: Given a fixed area of 36 square units, find rectangles whose sides multiply to 36 and draw each, labelling the sides.
List the factor pairs discovered: 2×18, 3×12, 4×9, 6×6 — all have area 36 (and 1×36 is also valid).
Check each rectangle against a grid to confirm it really covers 36 squares.
State what stays the same across all of them (the product/area = 36) and what changes (the shape).
activities.insight: One area can be made by many different rectangles; it is the product of the side lengths, not the shape, that is fixed.

activities.title: Area versus perimeter: surface versus edge
steps: For a 7 × 9 rectangle, work out both the area (multiply: 63 cm²) and the perimeter (add the sides around: 7 + 9 + 7 + 9 = 32 cm).
Say in words what each measures: area covers the surface in square units; perimeter is the distance around in linear units.
Given a mixed set of problems, decide for each whether to multiply (area) or add the edges (perimeter) and justify the choice.
Explain why a friend who did 8 + 5 = 13 for the garden's area has found something other than the area.
activities.insight: Area (surface, square units) and perimeter (distance around, linear units) are different measures computed differently; multiplying finds area, adding the edges finds perimeter.

activities.title: Check your understanding: compute, select, and label units
steps: Compute the area of a given rectangle and write it with correct square units (fill-in or short answer).
From several rectangles, select the one(s) with area 36, including a distractor whose perimeter is 36 (an 'add the sides' trap) but whose area is not 36.
Choose the correct unit for an area (cm vs cm²) and explain why.
Solve a word problem: a garden 8 m by 5 m — give the area with units (40 m²).
activities.insight: Applying area-as-product fluently means multiplying (not adding), using square units, and recognising correct rectangles for a target area.

checkQuestion: Pose three tasks: 'Find the area of a 7 cm by 9 cm rectangle'; 'Draw a rectangle with an area of 36 square units and label its sides'; and 'A garden is 8 m by 5 m — what is its area?' Watch whether they multiply (not add) the sides, whether they use square units, and whether they can reverse the relationship to construct a given area.
checkAnswer: The child multiplies the side lengths (7×9 = 63 cm²; 8×5 = 40 m²), states the answer in square units, and for the reverse task draws a valid rectangle whose sides multiply to 36 (e.g. 4×9 or 6×6) with sides labelled.
